7. Percent ionization and dilution

Degree and percent ionization

For a monoprotic acid or one-proton base, without added product ions and with negligible water contribution. The denominator is the initial concentration of the stated solute.

Diluting the same weak acid at constant temperature

For the same weak acid at constant temperature, dilution without interfering equilibria leaves the constant unchanged, increases percent ionization and decreases acid-produced hydronium concentration.

The amount of solute in moles remains unchanged, provided no solute is added or lost.
Add the moles of the same solute and divide by the actual final solution volume.
Adding water always decreases the amount of solute in moles in proportion to its concentration.
The two concentrations can always be averaged, even when the mixed volumes differ.

When a substance dissolves in water, its particles may remain as molecules or form ions. Substances that supply mobile ions and allow the solution to conduct electricity are called . Sucrose remains mainly as molecules and is . Dissolved sodium chloride separates essentially completely into ions and is , whereas ethanoic acid and ammonia form ions only partially and are each . A strong electrolyte is not necessarily a strong acid.

A solution must be described in terms of both and . For an acid, the first describes its tendency to donate a proton in water; the second describes the amount of substance per solution volume. A strong acid can therefore be dilute. Lamp comparisons require controlled concentration, temperature and apparatus, together with consideration of ion mobility.

The strong acids and bases considered here undergo essentially ionization or dissociation. An Initial–Change–Final, or ICF, table can therefore track amounts using the balanced equation. The amount in moles is found from , and molar concentration from , with volume in litres. Equation coefficients determine the solute-to-ion ratio: one mole of dissolved barium hydroxide, for example, supplies two moles of hydroxide ions.

Dilution without reaction or loss of solute relies on the following principle: When solutions of the same solute are mixed without reaction, their concentrations cannot simply be added:

Weak acids and bases react only partially with water, so unchanged solute and ions coexist at equilibrium. An Initial–Change–Equilibrium, or ICE, table tracks the initial concentrations, their changes and their equilibrium values. An equilibrium-constant expression uses concentrations throughout and omits pure liquid water as the solvent.

For a monoprotic weak acid with no added product ions and a negligible contribution from water, let be the initial concentration and the concentration ionized. Then . An analogous expression uses and hydroxide concentration for a weak base that accepts one proton. Percentage ionization compares with the solute concentration, rather than with the concentration of unchanged solute at equilibrium.

Replacing with requires the ionized amount to be compared with the initial concentration. This lesson uses an initial-concentration-to-constant ratio greater than one thousand as a preliminary screen. After calculating, apply the following check: If the check fails, The square-root approximation should therefore not be used for every weak acid or base without checking its conditions.

For the same weak acid at constant temperature, dilution without common ions or interfering equilibria has the following effects: Percentage ionization is a fraction of the original solute, so it need not change in the same direction as the ion concentration.

1. Electrolytes

An electrolyte is

A substance that provides mobile ions when dissolved in water or molten, allowing the liquid to conduct electricity.

A strong electrolyte · examples

The dissolved portion produces ions essentially completely, e.g. .

A weak electrolyte · examples

Produces ions only partially and establishes equilibrium, e.g. .

A nonelectrolyte · examples

Dissolves as molecules without producing appreciable solute ions, e.g. sucrose.

Conductivity comparisons must control

Concentration, temperature and the apparatus. Conductivity depends on both the amount and mobility of ions.

Strength describes proton transfer in water; concentration describes amount per volume. Strength alone cannot determine when initial concentrations differ.

Summary article A · From dissolved particles to strong-acid and strong-base calculations

The amount of solute in moles remains unchanged, provided no solute is added or lost.
Add the moles of the same solute and divide by the actual final solution volume.
Adding water always decreases the amount of solute in moles in proportion to its concentration.
The two concentrations can always be averaged, even when the mixed volumes differ.

When a substance dissolves in water, its particles may remain as molecules or form ions. Substances that supply mobile ions and allow the solution to conduct electricity are called electrolytes. Sucrose remains mainly as molecules and is a nonelectrolyte. Dissolved sodium chloride separates essentially completely into ions and is a strong electrolyte, whereas ethanoic acid and ammonia form ions only partially and are each a weak electrolyte. A strong electrolyte is not necessarily a strong acid.

A solution must be described in terms of both strength and concentration. For an acid, the first describes its tendency to donate a proton in water; the second describes the amount of substance per solution volume. A strong acid can therefore be dilute. Lamp comparisons require controlled concentration, temperature and apparatus, together with consideration of ion mobility.

Kru nix-centuryPage 1 / 41
CHEMISTRY · 10.3 · Ionization of acids, bases and waterExit Ticket Revision · Teacher answers

The strong acids and bases considered here undergo essentially complete ionization or dissociation. An Initial–Change–Final, or ICF, table can therefore track amounts using the balanced equation. The amount in moles is found from , and molar concentration from , with volume in litres. Equation coefficients determine the solute-to-ion ratio: one mole of dissolved barium hydroxide, for example, supplies two moles of hydroxide ions.

Dilution without reaction or loss of solute relies on the following principle: The amount of solute in moles remains unchanged, provided no solute is added or lost. When solutions of the same solute are mixed without reaction, their concentrations cannot simply be added: Add the moles of the same solute and divide by the actual final solution volume.

Weak acids and bases react only partially with water, so unchanged solute and ions coexist at equilibrium. An Initial–Change–Equilibrium, or ICE, table tracks the initial concentrations, their changes and their equilibrium values. An equilibrium-constant expression uses equilibrium concentrations throughout and omits pure liquid water as the solvent.

For a monoprotic weak acid with no added product ions and a negligible contribution from water, let be the initial concentration and the concentration ionized. Then . An analogous expression uses and hydroxide concentration for a weak base that accepts one proton. Percentage ionization compares with the initial solute concentration, rather than with the concentration of unchanged solute at equilibrium.

Replacing with requires the ionized amount to be very small compared with the initial concentration. This lesson uses an initial-concentration-to-constant ratio greater than one thousand as a preliminary screen. After calculating, apply the following check: Check the ionized fraction against the initial concentration; this lesson accepts the approximation when the calculated percentage is no more than about five percent. If the check fails, Use the full equilibrium equation and select the chemically meaningful root. The square-root approximation should therefore not be used for every weak acid or base without checking its conditions.

For the same weak acid at constant temperature, dilution without common ions or interfering equilibria has the following effects: The ionization constant stays the same, the percentage ionization increases, and the hydronium concentration supplied by the acid decreases. Percentage ionization is a fraction of the original solute, so it need not change in the same direction as the ion concentration.

Sentence Bank

A neutral solution must always have the same two ion concentrations as it does at twenty-five degrees Celsius.
A solution is neutral when its hydronium and hydroxide concentrations are equal; their values depend on temperature.

An acid that can donate more than one proton per molecule is a polyprotic acid. Proton donation is stepwise, with a separate equilibrium equation and constant for each step. If the first step supplies far more ions than later steps, a later contribution may be neglected after comparison. Sulfuric acid illustrates the need for care: its first ionization is treated as essentially complete, but The second ionization is an equilibrium, so sulfuric acid does not always supply twice its initial concentration of hydronium ions.

Water produces small amounts of hydronium and hydroxide ions. The relation

gives one ion concentration when the other is known. The ion product of water varies with temperature and equals at , so the value must match the conditions in the question. The neutrality criterion is: A solution is neutral when its hydronium and hydroxide concentrations are equal; their values depend on temperature. A higher hydronium concentration indicates an acidic solution; a higher hydroxide concentration indicates a basic solution.

Two species that differ by one proton and interconvert by proton transfer form a conjugate acid–base pair. The relation has an essential condition: The acid and base must form a conjugate pair in water at the same temperature. It follows that At the same temperature, an acid with a larger ionization constant has a conjugate base with a smaller ionization constant. Identify the conjugate pair and temperature before using this relation, rather than combining constants from unrelated acids and bases.

Revision Notes · 10.3

Read these notes and worked examples to help solve the front questions, then write your own Knowledge Recall.

1. Electrolytes

An electrolyte is

A substance that provides mobile ions when dissolved in water or molten, allowing the liquid to conduct electricity.

A strong electrolyte · examples

The dissolved portion produces ions essentially completely, e.g. .

A weak electrolyte · examples

Produces ions only partially and establishes equilibrium, e.g. .

A nonelectrolyte · examples

Dissolves as molecules without producing appreciable solute ions, e.g. sucrose.

Conductivity comparisons must control

Concentration, temperature and the apparatus. Conductivity depends on both the amount and mobility of ions.

2. Strong and weak acids and bases

Strong acids in this lesson

; only the first ionization of is treated as complete.

Strong bases in this lesson

. The dissolved portion dissociates essentially completely; strength and solubility are different properties.

Weak acids and bases · reaction arrows

Weak acids such as and weak bases such as use ; essentially complete ion formation uses .

How strength differs from concentration

Strength describes proton transfer in water; concentration describes amount per volume. Strength alone cannot determine when initial concentrations differ.

7. Percent ionization and dilution

Degree and percent ionization

For a monoprotic acid or one-proton base, without added product ions and with negligible water contribution. The denominator is the initial concentration of the stated solute.

Diluting the same weak acid at constant temperature

For the same weak acid at constant temperature, dilution without interfering equilibria leaves the constant unchanged, increases percent ionization and decreases acid-produced hydronium concentration.

8. Polyprotic acids

Stepwise equilibria and constants

The qualification

The first step is essentially complete, but is an equilibrium. Hydronium concentration is not always twice the analytical acid concentration.

If the first step dominates and , estimate and compare it with first-step hydronium before neglecting the extra contribution.

10. Conjugate acid–base constants

Relation and conditions

Use a conjugate pair in water at the same temperature.

Strengths within a conjugate pair

At the same temperature, the acid with larger has a conjugate base with smaller .

Derivation

Multiply the two expressions and cancel the conjugate-pair concentrations common to numerator and denominator.

Adding the reactions and cancelling the common species gives water autoionization.

This applies to a conjugate pair in water at the same temperature, using the school-level concentration treatment in place of activities.

Summary article A · From dissolved particles to strong-acid and strong-base calculations

Sentence Bank

The amount of solute in moles remains unchanged, provided no solute is added or lost.
Add the moles of the same solute and divide by the actual final solution volume.
Adding water always decreases the amount of solute in moles in proportion to its concentration.
The two concentrations can always be averaged, even when the mixed volumes differ.

When a substance dissolves in water, its particles may remain as molecules or form ions. Substances that supply mobile ions and allow the solution to conduct electricity are called electrolytes. Sucrose remains mainly as molecules and is a nonelectrolyte. Dissolved sodium chloride separates essentially completely into ions and is a strong electrolyte, whereas ethanoic acid and ammonia form ions only partially and are each a weak electrolyte. A strong electrolyte is not necessarily a strong acid.

A solution must be described in terms of both strength and concentration. For an acid, the first describes its tendency to donate a proton in water; the second describes the amount of substance per solution volume. A strong acid can therefore be dilute. Lamp comparisons require controlled concentration, temperature and apparatus, together with consideration of ion mobility.

Kru nix-centuryPage 1 / 31
CHEMISTRY · 10.3 · Ionization of acids, bases and waterExit Ticket Revision · Teacher answers

The strong acids and bases considered here undergo essentially complete ionization or dissociation. An Initial–Change–Final, or ICF, table can therefore track amounts using the balanced equation. The amount in moles is found from , and molar concentration from , with volume in litres. Equation coefficients determine the solute-to-ion ratio: one mole of dissolved barium hydroxide, for example, supplies two moles of hydroxide ions.

Dilution without reaction or loss of solute relies on the following principle: The amount of solute in moles remains unchanged, provided no solute is added or lost. When solutions of the same solute are mixed without reaction, their concentrations cannot simply be added: Add the moles of the same solute and divide by the actual final solution volume.

Weak acids and bases react only partially with water, so unchanged solute and ions coexist at equilibrium. An Initial–Change–Equilibrium, or ICE, table tracks the initial concentrations, their changes and their equilibrium values. An equilibrium-constant expression uses equilibrium concentrations throughout and omits pure liquid water as the solvent.

For a monoprotic weak acid with no added product ions and a negligible contribution from water, let be the initial concentration and the concentration ionized. Then . An analogous expression uses and hydroxide concentration for a weak base that accepts one proton. Percentage ionization compares with the initial solute concentration, rather than with the concentration of unchanged solute at equilibrium.

Kru nix-centuryPage 2 / 31
CHEMISTRY · 10.3 · Ionization of acids, bases and waterExit Ticket Revision · Teacher answers

Replacing with requires the ionized amount to be very small compared with the initial concentration. This lesson uses an initial-concentration-to-constant ratio greater than one thousand as a preliminary screen. After calculating, apply the following check: Check the ionized fraction against the initial concentration; this lesson accepts the approximation when the calculated percentage is no more than about five percent. If the check fails, Use the full equilibrium equation and select the chemically meaningful root. The square-root approximation should therefore not be used for every weak acid or base without checking its conditions.

For the same weak acid at constant temperature, dilution without common ions or interfering equilibria has the following effects: The ionization constant stays the same, the percentage ionization increases, and the hydronium concentration supplied by the acid decreases. Percentage ionization is a fraction of the original solute, so it need not change in the same direction as the ion concentration.

Sentence Bank

A neutral solution must always have the same two ion concentrations as it does at twenty-five degrees Celsius.
A solution is neutral when its hydronium and hydroxide concentrations are equal; their values depend on temperature.
The second ionization is an equilibrium, so sulfuric acid does not always supply twice its initial concentration of hydronium ions.
The acid and base must form a conjugate pair in water at the same temperature.
An acid with a larger ionization constant must also have a conjugate base with a larger ionization constant.
At the same temperature, an acid with a larger ionization constant has a conjugate base with a smaller ionization constant.
Any acid can be paired with any base, regardless of solvent or temperature.
Every acid with two hydrogen atoms always supplies twice its initial concentration of hydronium ions.

An acid that can donate more than one proton per molecule is a polyprotic acid. Proton donation is stepwise, with a separate equilibrium equation and constant for each step. If the first step supplies far more ions than later steps, a later contribution may be neglected after comparison. Sulfuric acid illustrates the need for care: its first ionization is treated as essentially complete, but The second ionization is an equilibrium, so sulfuric acid does not always supply twice its initial concentration of hydronium ions.

Water produces small amounts of hydronium and hydroxide ions. The relation

gives one ion concentration when the other is known. The ion product of water varies with temperature and equals at , so the value must match the conditions in the question. The neutrality criterion is: A solution is neutral when its hydronium and hydroxide concentrations are equal; their values depend on temperature. A higher hydronium concentration indicates an acidic solution; a higher hydroxide concentration indicates a basic solution.

Two species that differ by one proton and interconvert by proton transfer form a conjugate acid–base pair. The relation has an essential condition: The acid and base must form a conjugate pair in water at the same temperature. It follows that At the same temperature, an acid with a larger ionization constant has a conjugate base with a smaller ionization constant. Identify the conjugate pair and temperature before using this relation, rather than combining constants from unrelated acids and bases.

Revision Notes · 10.3

Read these notes and worked examples to help solve the front questions, then write your own Knowledge Recall.

1. Electrolytes

An electrolyte is

A substance that provides mobile ions when dissolved in water or molten, allowing the liquid to conduct electricity.

A strong electrolyte · examples

The dissolved portion produces ions essentially completely, e.g. .

A weak electrolyte · examples

Produces ions only partially and establishes equilibrium, e.g. .

A nonelectrolyte · examples

Dissolves as molecules without producing appreciable solute ions, e.g. sucrose.

Conductivity comparisons must control

Concentration, temperature and the apparatus. Conductivity depends on both the amount and mobility of ions.

2. Strong and weak acids and bases

Strong acids in this lesson

; only the first ionization of is treated as complete.

Strong bases in this lesson

. The dissolved portion dissociates essentially completely; strength and solubility are different properties.

Weak acids and bases · reaction arrows

Weak acids such as and weak bases such as use ; essentially complete ion formation uses .

How strength differs from concentration

Strength describes proton transfer in water; concentration describes amount per volume. Strength alone cannot determine when initial concentrations differ.

4. ICF and dilution

ICF stands for · use it when

Initial – Change – Final. Use for essentially complete dissociation, following the balanced equation and consistent units.

What stays constant during dilution

The amount of the original solute is conserved when none is added or lost.

Mixing solutions of the same solute

Add amounts of the same solute and divide by actual final solution volume, provided no reaction consumes that solute.

7. Percent ionization and dilution

Degree and percent ionization

For a monoprotic acid or one-proton base, without added product ions and with negligible water contribution. The denominator is the initial concentration of the stated solute.

Diluting the same weak acid at constant temperature

For the same weak acid at constant temperature, dilution without interfering equilibria leaves the constant unchanged, increases percent ionization and decreases acid-produced hydronium concentration.

8. Polyprotic acids

Stepwise equilibria and constants

The qualification

The first step is essentially complete, but is an equilibrium. Hydronium concentration is not always twice the analytical acid concentration.

If the first step dominates and , estimate and compare it with first-step hydronium before neglecting the extra contribution.

10. Conjugate acid–base constants

Relation and conditions

Use a conjugate pair in water at the same temperature.

Strengths within a conjugate pair

At the same temperature, the acid with larger has a conjugate base with smaller .

Derivation

Multiply the two expressions and cancel the conjugate-pair concentrations common to numerator and denominator.

Adding the reactions and cancelling the common species gives water autoionization.

This applies to a conjugate pair in water at the same temperature, using the school-level concentration treatment in place of activities.

Knowledge Recall

1. Electrolytes and strength

A. Define an electrolyte and identify its charge carriers.

A substance providing mobile ions; the ions carry current.

B. Distinguish strong electrolytes, weak electrolytes and nonelectrolytes.

Essentially complete / partial / negligible solute-ion formation.

C. Distinguish acid strength from solution concentration.

Strength describes proton transfer in water; concentration describes amount per volume. Strength alone cannot determine when initial concentrations differ.

2. Moles, complete dissociation and dilution

A. Write formulas for amount from mass and for solution concentration.

B. Name the stages in a complete-dissociation table and state when to use it.

Initial – Change – Final. Use for essentially complete dissociation, following the balanced equation and consistent units.

C. Write the dilution relation and name the conserved quantity.

The amount of the original solute stays constant when none is added or lost.

3. Weak acids/bases and equilibrium tables

A. Name the stages in an equilibrium concentration table and state the unit of the concentration change.

Initial – Change – Equilibrium; is a concentration change in when the table uses concentrations.

B. Write the reactions of a weak monoprotic acid and a weak one-proton base with water.

C. Write the acid and base ionization constant expressions and state which concentrations they require.

Use equilibrium concentrations throughout; pure solvent water is omitted.
At the same temperature, a larger indicates a stronger base in water.
